problemText: In Federalist No. 10 (1787), James Madison writes that a faction is a group of citizens "united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community." Madison's central worry in this definition is best described as concern that —
choices: a minority faction could seize permanent control of the national government through a violent coup
state governments would refuse to send delegates to the Constitutional Convention
narrow group interests could override the rights of others or the public good
foreign nations would exploit factions to install a monarchy in the United States
hints: Notice the two things Madison says a faction's impulse is 'adverse to' — the rights of other citizens, and the community's shared interests.
Rule out any answer describing a coup, a convention boycott, or foreign monarchy — none of those appear in Madison's definition.

problemText: Brutus No. 1 (1787), an Anti-Federalist essay, warns that "History furnishes no example of a free republic, any thing like the extent of the United States." This claim most directly reflects the Anti-Federalist position that —
choices: a republic spanning so vast a territory could not preserve free government
the new Constitution granted the president too little authority over foreign affairs
history offered no precedent at all for any form of representative government
the thirteen states were too small individually ever to resist British reconquest
hints: Brutus is pointing to the sheer size of the United States as the problem, not any single institution or power.
Brutus concedes small republics (Greek, Roman) existed — the objection is specifically about extending a republic over so large a territory.

problemText: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argues an extended republic best controls faction, since citizens are less likely to be "united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest" across a large territory. Brutus No. 1 responds by pointing to the ancient world, warning that once the Greek and Roman republics grew too large, "their governments were changed from that of free governments to those of the most tyrannical that ever existed in the world." Compared to Madison, Brutus's argument about the size of a republic —
choices: reaches the same conclusion, that a large republic best protects liberty by diluting the power of any single faction
does not address the size of the republic at all, focusing only on judicial power
agrees with Madison but argues Congress, not the size of the republic, is the true safeguard against faction
reaches the opposite conclusion: extending a republic's territory too far tends to destroy free government rather than protect it
hints: Madison treats a large territory as the cure for faction; ask what Brutus says a large territory does to free government instead.
Brutus is an Anti-Federalist essay opposing ratification — expect it to directly contradict a core Federalist argument, not restate or sidestep it.

problemText: In Federalist No. 51 (1788), James Madison writes, "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition." This statement most directly expresses which constitutional design principle?
choices: judicial review, allowing federal courts to strike down unconstitutional acts of state legislatures
checks and balances, giving each branch tools to resist encroachment by the others
federalism, dividing government power between the national government and the individual state governments
popular sovereignty, requiring elected officials to win their offices directly from the voters
hints: Madison wants one branch's self-interest to actively resist another branch's overreach — that is a description of a mechanism, not a source of legal authority.
Rule out federalism (national vs. state), judicial review (courts vs. legislatures), and elections (voters vs. officials) — none of those is 'ambition counteracting ambition' within one government.

problemText: Federalist No. 51 continues, "If men were angels, no Government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on Government would be necessary." Madison offers this reasoning to justify which conclusion?
choices: Most citizens are so virtuous that legal restraints on officials are rarely necessary
Because angels do not exist, republican government can never realistically be sustained in practice
Human nature cannot be changed, so a strong monarchy is the only workable government
Government power must be limited by formal checks, not trust in official virtue
hints: Madison's 'if men were angels' is a hypothetical he immediately rejects — people and officials are not angels.
The conclusion should follow logically from 'people are not perfectly virtuous,' not assert something about monarchy or the impossibility of republics.

problemText: Federalist No. 51 explains that "the power surrendered by the People is first divided between two distinct Governments, and then the portion allotted to each, subdivided among distinct and separate departments. Hence a double security arises to the rights of the People." The "two distinct Governments" in this "double security" argument refer to —
choices: the House of Representatives and the Senate
the Federalist and Anti-Federalist political factions
the national government and the state governments
the executive branch and the judicial branch
hints: Madison describes power being divided first, and only afterward subdivided again among departments — that first division is the federalism layer, not the separation-of-powers layer.
Rule out any answer naming branches or houses of one government — the passage is describing two separate governments, national and state.

problemText: A federal budget data table shows total grants-in-aid to state and local governments, measured in constant (inflation-adjusted) dollars, rising every year sampled: from roughly 256 billion in 1990, to 416 billion in 2000, to 680 billion in 2010, to 692 billion in 2019. Over that same span, grants-in-aid as a percentage of total federal outlays rose from 10.8% in 1990 to a peak of 17.6% in 2010, before easing to 16.2% by 2019. Which statement is best supported by this data?
choices: Inflation-adjusted grant dollars rose throughout, while the grants' share of outlays peaked in 2010, not 2019
Both the inflation-adjusted grant dollars and the grants' share of federal outlays rose without interruption across the whole period
Grants-in-aid outlays only became a meaningfully large share of the total federal budget sometime after the year 2010
Inflation-adjusted grant dollars fell after 2010, even though the grants' share of federal outlays kept rising through 2019
hints: Track the dollar figures and the percentage figures as two separate trends — one rises every year shown, the other does not.
The percentage column rises, then falls back slightly by 2019 — find the single year given as its highest point.

problemText: The same federal budget table reports that of the 692 billion dollars in federal grants-in-aid outlays in fiscal year 2019, about 581 billion dollars (84%) came as categorical grants — funds restricted to narrowly defined purposes and often carrying matching or compliance requirements — while about 111 billion dollars (16%) came as block grants, which give states broader discretion over how funds are spent. This breakdown best supports which conclusion about federal grants-in-aid in 2019?
choices: States had complete legal discretion over how every federal grant dollar they received was spent
Most federal grant dollars carried federally defined conditions, leaving states comparatively little spending discretion
The federal government provided no grant funding to state or local governments in 2019
Block grants made up a larger total dollar value than categorical grants in fiscal year 2019
hints: Compare the two dollar figures directly — one type of grant is roughly five times larger than the other.
Categorical grants come with compliance requirements attached; ask what that means for how much discretion states have over most of the money.

problemText: The federal budget table shows categorical grants — funds Congress restricts to narrowly defined purposes with compliance requirements attached — making up 84% of federal grants-in-aid dollars in fiscal year 2019. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court held that Congress may use means not explicitly listed in the Constitution, so long as they are a reasonable way to carry out an enumerated power. Applying this reasoning, Congress's authority to attach detailed conditions to categorical grants is best understood as an exercise of —
choices: an enumerated power expressly listed in Article I, Section 8, requiring no further constitutional justification
inherent authority the president holds independently of Congress and the courts under Article II
implied power under the Necessary and Proper Clause, advancing Congress's spending and taxing powers
a reserved power belonging exclusively to the states under the Tenth Amendment
hints: Nothing in Article I, Section 8 explicitly lists a power to 'attach conditions to grants' — so the authority must come from somewhere else, the way chartering a bank did in McCulloch.
Reserved powers belong to the states, and Article II authority belongs to the president — neither fits a power Congress is exercising over its own spending.

problemText: The federal budget table shows that federal grants-in-aid to state and local governments reached 692 billion dollars in fiscal year 2019, the large majority delivered as categorical grants with conditions attached, rather than through direct federal regulation of state governments. In United States v. Lopez (1995), the Supreme Court held that Congress's power under the Commerce Clause does not extend to regulating activity, like carrying a gun near a school, that is not itself economic. Given Lopez's limits on direct federal regulation under the Commerce Clause, Congress's heavy reliance on conditional grants-in-aid instead of direct regulation is best explained by which reasoning?
choices: Lopez eliminated Congress's spending power entirely, so grants-in-aid became the only tool of federal influence left after 1995
Conditional spending lets Congress shape state policy beyond the Commerce Clause's reach, since states may freely decline the funds
The Necessary and Proper Clause was struck down in Lopez, forcing Congress to rely solely on treaties with individual states
States are constitutionally required to accept any federal grant offered to them, no matter its attached conditions or cost
hints: Lopez limits one specific power (the Commerce Clause) — it says nothing about Congress's separate spending power.
Grants-in-aid are voluntary: states can decline federal money and its conditions, which is exactly what makes conditional spending a distinct tool from direct regulation.
